#645. NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble's high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.

By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.

The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.

Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.

Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.

But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.

Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.

These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov

Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

NASA's Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.

Hubble and Webb observations complement each other, providing us with a broad view of the universe.

#644. China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway

There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives, is the message.

Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.

All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?

The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.

As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said, “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”

But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)

China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes. “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.

Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians, including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “LinkedIn espionage”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives.

Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business. The Biden administration had sharply limited the export of cutting-edge chips globally to slow China’s development of AI, but Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen those restrictions.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Donald Trump denied having prior knowledge of Alice Huang’s potential espionage. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” On Tuesday, the Times reported that Marco Rubio had briefed Trump in May, right before Jensen Huang joined the president on Air Force One for a trip to China.

The veracity of Trump's claims will surely be investigated, especially in the context of the famous Watergate maxim: “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Nvidia’s CEO has been publicly linked to the Megaspeed executive since at least 2024 and Alice’s husband, Kang Weigh, has reportedly known Jensen since the 2010s. WIRED’s Lauren Goode reported on Monday that Jensen Huang, starting in 2025, hired Risa Heller’s crisis communications firm, which is well-versed in handling public sex scandals. This spring, secretary of state Marco Rubio evidently helped craft a classified memo inside the administration warning officials about Jensen Huang’s potentially compromising relationship.

Jensen Huang—who has developed an important reputation as AI’s number one cheerleader at the frontier of AI labs—is now stuck in an awkward situation. Is he an idiot, unaware that his paramour might have been a foreign intelligence asset? Merely reckless with his own reputation, fiduciary responsibility to Nvidia, and the technological security of the United States? Or a witting accomplice to undermining US national security?

Regardless of the truth, Nvidia loses. Shareholders have ridden a roller-coaster that has seen Nvidia’s stock rise by about 600 percent over the past five years, becoming the world’s second-most valuable company. In the past month, the stock has plummeted by a quarter. The disaster for Nvidia is just beginning, it seems, as lawsuits loom, including by its own shareholders.

Similarly, the Trump administration is likely to face real questions from the newly Democratic congress: When were the president and other top officials briefed about this intelligence threat? What communication, if any, did they make to Nvidia and to whom? Should more have been done by US intelligence to block Alice Huang from having access to Nvidia and its CEO?

The fact that Megaspeed is a major customer of Nvidia makes everything more complicated. Indeed, reports have circulated for at least a year that the US was concerned that Megaspeed was diverting chips to Chinese intelligence agencies, an allegation that could have massive consequences for the global AI race. Bloomberg this week reported that Megaspeed's subsidiaries have purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and that an audit requested by the US government last year found that Megaspeed couldn’t initially account for some 50,000 chips it had purchased.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang and President Trump developed a uniquely close professional relationship. They’ve met multiple times as Huang has pushed to loosen Biden-era export controls, which Trump has repeatedly relaxed; Huang has donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project; while en route to Beijing earlier this year with a delegation of tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook, Trump’s Air Force One actually made a special stop in Alaska to pick up Huang; Huang also attended a White House state dinner for Chinese president Xi Jinping and Trump, who in turn, awarded him a National Medal of Science earlier this fall.

The implication that Trump knew and did nothing for a year would make this one of the greatest counterintelligence failures of the past decade. There will be consequences: Across history, many have gone to prison for honeypot scandals; a former adviser was arrested just last year in a similar plot; though he was acquitted of committing economic espionage, he was convicted for making false statements to investigators.

Even in normal circumstances, corporate America’s tolerance of CEO misbehavior has shrunken dramatically. In recent years, CEOs at companies as varied as Nestlé, Kohl’s, BP, NBCUniversal, and the railroad Norfolk Southern have all resigned or been forced out after inappropriate relationships that violated company standards.

If Nvidia were any other company and Jensen Huang any other CEO, the facts of the scandal currently known would be enough to topple some heads. But Trump is still president, and November is only a third over. It’s not even clear that this will rank as the biggest scandal of the month—but it should.

#643. Expedia CEO says AI agents aren't changing booking habits — yet

Expedia CEO Ariane Gorin said Thursday the company hasn't yet seen artificial intelligence agents affecting the way customers book, but the early signs show potential for an industry shift.

"It's a great way for people to do inspiration, to do trip planning," Gorin said in an interview with CNBC. "We haven't seen it change the way they're actually doing booking."

The comments come as personal AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots enter the mainstream, promising to tackle everything from scheduling to shopping for everyday Americans. Opportunities in travel planning and booking could pose a competitive threat to traditional sites like Expedia.

Gorin said Expedia is "working with all of the agents" to make sure it surfaces in AI results, to understand how the agents get information and to make sure that the company has the necessary integrations.

She acknowledged it's possible that AI agents could develop their own travel programs and eventually claim market share, but she said complexities within the industry — customer service, for example — would be difficult to fully replace with artificial intelligence.

"People were already shopping across a number of places, so the agent can do that in a much easier way," Gorin said. "But when it comes to actually booking — being confident that the content that you're getting is right, the amenities are right, the price is right, if something goes wrong, someone's going to actually either solve it for you, answer the phone, be there for you — I don't think those agents are going to do it for you, and that's why people trust Expedia and come to us."

Shares of Expedia were down about 12% Thursday after the company delivered weaker-than-expected guidance for the fourth quarter on Wednesday. The company forecast revenue of between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion for the final three months of the year, making the midpoint lower than analyst estimates of $3.74 billion, according to FactSet.

Gorin attributed the "moderation" in Expedia's fourth-quarter guidance to "geopolitical events in the Middle East and Europe," the midterm elections and the company moving its fall sale from the fourth quarter to the third quarter. But she noted the company reported a strong third quarter, as total gross bookings rose 11% and revenue climbed 12%.

#642. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

#641. The AO3 Shutdown Is Pitting Fanfic Readers Against Authors

Avery has been writing fan fiction for about six years, now mainly focused on the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry. Until last month, it all lived in one place—Archive of Our Own. Then, on October 29 the fan fiction behemoth went dark due to a “security incident.” Within days, Avery was alarmed to find her works on mirror sites she hadn’t posted them to.

“To me it’s a security risk,” Avery, who did not want her real name used due to fears of backlash on social media, tells WIRED via DM. “One bad actor could put malware in that drive.”

She emailed the sites—Squidgeworld and AO3.Life—and the stories were removed, though she’ll never know if she has found every copy online. (AO3.Life has since been taken down, and Walter Hopgood, president of Squidge.org, which hosts Squidgeworld, told WIRED it removes works that are posted without an author’s permission.)

Avery’s problem is one shared with many fanfic authors since the team behind AO3 announced the site will remain offline for up to four weeks.

Hosting more than 18.8 million fan works across hundreds of thousands of fandoms, AO3 is among the most visited websites in the world. When it went down, some fans started freaking out over the “AO3 apocalypse.” Within days, readers who had saved stories on their own device placed them onto shared libraries on Google Drives. But finding alternatives has caused friction in the community, as some authors are unhappy with the way their works are being distributed without their permission, breaking fanfic norms and exacerbating fears about AI scraping.

One of the many drives to pop up was the Archive Salvation Google Drive project, a collective of fan fiction downloaded from AO3. It faced criticism after launching, though a spokesperson tells WIRED it offered ways for authors to ask for their work to be removed. But it’s since been hacked and is no longer accessible, according to a November 3 statement on a moderator’s TikTok, though the group behind it is still sharing fanfics in a closed Discord server.

“We continue to acknowledge the controversies of such drives but also want to acknowledge the joy this has brought readers and the authors who submitted their fics to us,” the statement said, adding, “our drive was controversial and very public, so the hacker is most likely someone who stands against drives like this in general.”

Avery doesn’t mind her work circulating in private drives or being asked for copies of their work for fans to read—her concern is with her work being uploaded to giant drive libraries.

But she says AO3’s breakdown has revealed entitlement among some readers, who’ve messaged her demanding to know where her fics are now available. “I just can’t wait for AO3 to go back up so that people can go back to normal,” she says. “It’s left a sour taste in my mouth.”

“Writers hating their readers this much will kill fandoms actually,” one user wrote on X in response to an artist expressing frustration about people who “don’t contribute anything to the fandom” weighing in on how work is shared. Another X user accused the same artist of being “self-righteous” and “entitled.”

Avery says some readers seem to feel authors’ feelings “are secondary to the readers.” “It feels like AO3 going down made so many people so crazy that they couldn’t get their fix, and I think the authors are most outspoken because it’s our work.”

Riley, who did not want their real name used for fear of receiving more backlash, made their X account private soon after.

“I did not anticipate the potential harmful effects of me compiling the document of stories, which is why I deleted it,” they tell WIRED.

Meanwhile, Ellipsus, a collaborative writing platform with an anti-AI stance that was founded in 2022, has seen a boom in interest since AO3 went down. Allegra Rosenberg, an Ellipsus employee and writer, says that new sign-ups are up more than 500 percent since the outage began and views of its public reader links—the ways in which authors can share work—have increased heavily.

What Ellipsus offers is control. Authors can control who can see their work and how they can interact with it. They can turn on comments, and readers can leave kudos (called “props” on Ellipsus), as well as custom fonts and themes. Rosenberg says the company noticed that many of the users were fan fiction writers and adjusted features for them before the outage, for example, a button that exports work directly to AO3.

”We know that people want a space to not only write but share new writing, in a way that feels safe for them,” says Rosenberg.

Another reason the outage has felt so fraught is that the world of fan fiction has broken containment, becoming mainstream in part due to shows like Heated Rivalry and the adaptation of former fan fictions such as Alchemised by SenLinYu, which was originally published on AO3, into bona fide novels.

“It’s the Tik-tokification of fanfic,” Avery says.“Everyone wants a snippet and a graphic and a one shot, and they can share it on Twitter, and then suddenly a thing I wrote years ago goes viral. Fan fiction never used to go viral.”

Rosenberg, who is writing a book on fandom, thinks that so much of the backlash comes from a mismatch between how big the community actually is and how small it still feels to many. The giant drives and libraries drew outrage due to their scale and a fear from many fans that their stories could be taken down. That fear has a real history within fandom spaces.

“In the ’90s and 2000s, there were cease-and-desist notices and takedown controversies on Fanfiction.net and LiveJournal that led to AO3’s founding,” Rosenberg explains. “So there is this shared history and memory within fandom culture as a whole when it comes to fan fiction.”

The demand for fan fiction does not come only from people active in fandom circles. It also comes from people who are seen as casual fans—those who are not as invested in the wider fandom. Fan fiction operates on norms where people ask permission, and there is a tolerance for a certain level of informal sharing. The AO3 outage has tested these norms and has exposed the lack of practical protection an author has once their work is posted. Readers are doing what they have always done—sharing work that they love. However, the burden of this sharing is uneven, as authors fear losing track of their own work.

“I think this whole AO3 going down thing has reminded people that the internet is forever for better or for worse,” Avery says. “Long after I die, if we still have the internet, my fics will float about even without AO3.”

#639. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#637. A Startup Wants to Fight AI Bioweapons With AI

Frontier AI labs have warned that their technology could help develop dangerous bioweapons.

Now, a startup says it has developed a defense. On Wednesday, Radical Numerics announced that it has developed a new edge model called Omnii Defense that is designed to flag natural and AI-engineered pathogens using a laptop and a USB gene sequencer. It can also run without an internet connection, allowing researchers in the field with spotty connections to use it. Though many scientists say AI-made bioweapons are a low-likelihood threat, Radical Numerics hopes its technology will help researchers and public health officials identify emerging biological threats.

Eric Nguyen, cofounder and CEO of Radical Numerics, says he sees a coming arms race in biodefense similar to what’s playing out in cybersecurity, where threat actors and security defenders are leveraging AI in an attempt to gain an edge.

“We felt that the biosecurity space was far behind on the defense side,” he says.

Nguyen and his cofounders were part of the research team behind Evo and Evo-2, open-source DNA foundation models they worked on during their doctoral research at Stanford University. They founded Radical Numerics in 2025.

The San Francisco–based company recently made waves after rolling out Omnii, a new genome language model built on different types of biological information beyond DNA, including RNA, proteins, and epigenetic signals. In October, Radical announced that it used Omnii to create custom bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill specific bacteria, targeting a drug-resistant strain of E. coli. Its cocktail was used to treat a sick patient, with special permission from the Food and Drug Administration.

Another AI biotech startup, Tabula Bioscience, was also involved in that research, but Radical didn’t disclose the partnership in its announcement last month. The omission led Harvard geneticist George Church, who was an adviser to both companies, to resign from his role at Radical last week.

Omnii Defense, the company’s latest tool, makes multiple predictions about a sequence, including the odds of it being pathogenic or AI-generated and what taxonomic group it most closely resembles. The model assigns a genome a “threat score” between zero and one that combines the likelihood of unnaturalness with functional predictions. The higher the score, the higher the threat.

Earlier biodefense tools, such as the federally funded Finding Engineering-Linked Indicators, or Felix, can compare genetic sequences of interest against libraries of known organisms, essentially searching for cataloged matches. That can be helpful in a scenario where a bad actor has made a few tweaks to an existing pathogen. But they aren’t designed to make predictions in the way that Omnii is.

The benefit of AI models is that they can learn patterns in sequences associated with biological function instead of relying on exact sequence matches. That could allow them to recognize similarities between sequences even when their genetic spelling has changed. Christine Parthemore, Radical Numerics’ head of biodefense, says Omnii is a “step change.”

In one experiment, the company removed Bundibugyo virus—which is currently driving an Ebola outbreak in East Africa—from the training data, first at the species level and then its whole genus. “It was as if Omnii was operating in 1976,” Parthemore says, referring to the year Ebola was discovered. With just the species removed, the model still detected that 33 percent of the Bundibugyo sequences pushed to it were something pathogenic. Even with the whole genus removed, it flagged 22 percent of the viral sequences. Non-AI tools gave essentially no indication of potential risk, she says.

“We absolutely need to be vigilant about what AI is enabling, and if we can use technology to compete with it and hopefully get ahead of any kind of nefarious actors, that seems sensible,” says Bronwyn MacInnis, director of pathogen surveillance in the Infectious Disease and Microbiome program at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.

However, MacInnis cautions that detecting a signal is still a big leap from determining whether a pathogen has real consequence or whether a threat was engineered.

Access to Omnii Defense is currently limited to vetted external testers. Radical Numerics says it is working with national laboratories, government agencies, and other independent evaluators to assess the model’s performance.

#635. I Am Artemis Katie Spicer

For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history.

Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives.

“I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.”

Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory, performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists.

“I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said.

From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station. She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed. It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations.

Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018. The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her. Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications.

“Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said. “On my own, I studied engineering principles. I passed boards and certification tests. I learned to speak ‘engineer!’”

Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight.

Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface.

“I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

#634. NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

After spending more than a year experiencing what life could be like on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally stepped outside, marking the end of an ambitious experiment designed to prepare humans for future missions to the Red Planet.

The crew completed their simulated Mars journey on October 31, 2026, emerging into the outside world for the first time in more than a year. Although the volunteers never actually left Earth, their extended mission recreated many of the challenges astronauts could encounter while living and working millions of miles from home.

The experiment was part of NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) program, which investigates how people adapt to the demanding conditions of extended space exploration.

The four volunteers were Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right). Following the completion of their mission, the crew posed together outdoors, celebrating their return from a simulated journey to another planet.

Throughout the experiment, the participants carried out tasks similar to those that future Mars explorers may need to perform. These included operating and testing essential systems, caring for crops, conserving limited supplies, and conducting extravehicular activities.

Extravehicular activities, often called spacewalks, are operations astronauts perform outside their spacecraft or habitat. In a Mars simulation, these activities help researchers examine how crews might prepare for and carry out work beyond the safety of their living quarters.

The volunteers also had to manage communication delays, an important challenge for anyone traveling to Mars. Unlike astronauts aboard the International Space Station, who can communicate with Earth almost instantly, future Mars explorers will experience significant delays because radio signals take time to cross the enormous distance between the two planets.

These delays mean astronauts cannot always depend on immediate guidance from mission control. They must be prepared to solve problems, make decisions, and manage unexpected situations with greater independence.

One of the biggest challenges of sending people to Mars is keeping them healthy, productive, and safe during long periods away from Earth. A crew must be able to manage food, equipment, living conditions, and daily responsibilities while working together in a confined environment.

NASA uses analog missions to explore these challenges before attempting actual journeys into deep space. An analog mission is a realistic simulation that reproduces selected conditions of space exploration while allowing scientists to study how people respond in a controlled setting on Earth.

The CHAPEA program provides an opportunity to investigate how astronauts might handle the practical demands of extended missions, including resource limitations, equipment maintenance, food production, and communication difficulties.

The lessons learned from Montgomery, Spicer, Elder, and Ellis will help NASA plan future human exploration missions. Their experiences are expected to inform the development of NASA's planned Moon Base and preparations for eventual crewed expeditions to Mars.

Although this crew's journey took place entirely on Earth, the knowledge gained could help address some of the challenges humans will face when they finally travel to the Red Planet.

#633. Wendy's rejects $1.4 billion takeover proposal from Nelson Peltz’s Trian

Wendy's on Thursday said it is rejecting a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management.

The group offered $7.35 per share in cash on Oct. 28 to take the struggling burger chain private. In addition to Trian, it included investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.

In February, Wendy's board formed a committee of independent directors to assess any potential bid from Trian in response to a regulatory filing from the firm. The committee found that the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's and does not reflect potential gains from the chain's ongoing turnaround strategy, the company said in a press release Thursday.

"Our confidence rests firmly in [CEO] Bob Wright's proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds," Art Winkleblack, Wendy's board chair and a member of the independent committee, said in a statement.

Trian declined to comment on Wendy's decision.

To stave off a hostile takeover, Wendy's has adopted a shareholder rights plan — or poison pill — with a one-year duration, as of Wednesday, the company said. Wendy's added that the investor group led by Trian rejected an offer from Wendy's for a standstill agreement that would have paused additional share purchases, adding to Wendy's decision to use a poison pill.

The rejection is the latest in the long-running saga between Peltz and the burger chain, which dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. A Peltz firm has even owned Wendy's before. In 2008, his company Triarc, which also owned Arby's, bought Wendy's in a $2.3 billion deal. It later sold Arby's, turning Wendy's into a stand-alone company again.

In 2024, Wendy's named Peltz as chairman emeritus after he spent 17 years on the company's board. Trian executive Peter May and Peltz's son, Bradley, still sit on Wendy's board.

Wendy's also reported its third-quarter results on Thursday. Its same-store sales declined for the seventh straight quarter. However, its quarterly earnings and revenue topped Wall Street's expectations.

Shares of Wendy's fell less than 1% in morning trading. The takeover offer had lifted the stock, which has lost about 60% of its value over the last three years.

Wendy's is not the only restaurant chain that has found itself in the crosshairs of activist investors. Applebee's owner Dine Brands recently adopted a poison pill to block a takeover bid from investment firms Arkhouse Management and Cobblers Cove Capital.

#630. 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.

Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.

"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."

The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.

Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.

A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor

Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.

Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.

Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.

"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."

The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.

"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.

The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.

"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."

As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.

The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.

Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.

Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.

Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle

The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.

Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.

First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.

"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."

The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.

To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.

The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.

Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.

The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.

The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

However, as preorders opened on Sept. 10, stock allocations sold out everywhere — especially the black version, which is sold exclusively via PlayStation Direct.

With both GTA 6 DualSense controllers scheduled for release on Nov. 19, several major stores still have preorder listings for the white edition, with intermittent restocks expected over the next week.

Be sure to keep this page bookmarked as we’ve checked across go-to retailers, confirmed where you can buy DualSense right now, and provided the full list of links you’ll need to check for the best chance of grabbing GTA 6’s limited edition controllers going forward.

Before GTA 6's launch on Nov. 19, these are the main retailers in the U.S. to bookmark and check for preorders:

PlayStation Direct (Black): Your only official U.S. retailer for the black controller. Sony has imposed a one-per-order limit, so don’t try to grab more than one if you’re lucky to get through.

PlayStation Direct (White): Also listed through Sony's storefront, the white version isn't exclusive. With that, there are several alternatives if PlayStation Direct runs out.

Amazon: A live listing for the white DualSense is available to buy now.

Walmart: The GTA 6 limited-edition PS5 DualSense controller is in stock at the time of writing. Shipping’s estimated to arrive on the game’s Nov. 19 release day.

Target: The white GTA 6 controller is in stock at the time of writing, though at the standard $84.99 price. The shipping date’s a little later than Walmart.

GameStop: Currently available to preorder online at $84.99. However, the delivery date is estimated for Nov. 20-25.

Best Buy: The white edition controller at $84.99 is out of stock online, but is currently marked as “Coming Soon."

GTA 6’s massive hype has undoubtedly led shoppers directly to the game’s dedicated PS5 DualSense controllers. It's the natural way of things.

As reported by IGN, 100 million PS5s have now been sold, including 2.1 million in the last quarter. It feels like a lot of recent sales have been driven by GTA 6. PC players need to wait, and the Xbox Series X|S’s install base pales in comparison to PlayStation, making the PS5 the default way to play GTA 6.

Not every one of the 100 million PS5 owners in the world will be playing GTA 6 or would even want the controller, but it does mean that the pool of potential buyers who’d want a dedicated GTA-themed DualSense controller is significant. Both controllers draw inspiration from GTA 6's fictional Vice City setting, though each represents a different side of the game's Florida-inspired location.

If the GTA 6 DualSense is unavailable, there are a few ways to make the search less frustrating:

Get your retailer accounts ready: Sign in to Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and PlayStation Direct ahead of time, with your payment and delivery information saved. That way, you won't have to scramble through checkout if new stock appears.

Remember PlayStation Direct’s exclusivity for the black controller: Since it's the only official U.S. retailer carrying this version, there's little benefit in searching elsewhere unless you're considering resale listings.

Use stock alerts where available: Retailer notifications and independent trackers can help flag when inventory is returning without requiring you to manually check every product page throughout the day.

Check local stores around launch: Best Buy, Target, and GameStop could be worth contacting starting Nov. 19. In-store inventory isn't guaranteed, but it offers another option if online orders become unavailable entirely.

Avoid paying collector prices too early: Both controllers have an official $84.99 recommended retail price. Listings substantially above that are not worthwhile while there's still a chance of additional stock reaching major stores.

It's possible, although Sony hasn't confirmed a dedicated Black Friday restock.

With GTA 6 launching on Nov. 19 and Black Friday 2026 taking place on Nov. 27, there's a relatively short gap between the release date and the biggest shopping event of the year. With that, retailers could receive more inventory around launch or hold additional units for the holiday shopping period. However, neither possibility is guaranteed, especially for the black controller, which remains exclusive to PlayStation Direct in the U.S.

Even if there were more stock in time for Black Friday, it doesn't necessarily mean these special editions will be discounted. Given their limited availability and high demand, retailers have no reason to knock anything off the price just yet. At this stage, selling out at MSRP is already almost a guarantee.

For now, the safest approach is to keep checking the retailer pages above and secure your preferred design if it becomes available at a reasonable price. Waiting until Black Friday might pay off, but there's a slim chance that either controller will still be available to buy after Nov. 19.

#627. I Saw the Future of Robotics in a Virtual Duck That Chases My Cat

Allow me to introduce you to the robot cat butler I’m developing with help from AI.

Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, I taught a virtual version of Microduck—a cute robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face—to walk around a room and identify any bengal cats in its vicinity. (The clip above shows the robot waddling toward a target feline; its eye view is shown top right.)

I’m still waiting patiently for a physical Microduck—please hurry up and ship it, guys—but simulated behavior is relatively simple, so it should transfer over to the real thing. I plan to have the robot automatically dispense a treat for my pet bengal, Leona, perhaps by bowing its head to release one from a 3D-printed, head-mounted storage chamber.

I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible. Previously, this kind of thing might have taken me weeks to figure out. It was possible because OpenAI’s latest models are remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and then translating that into useful code, agentic actions, and robot training.

Real roboticists are using the latest models to do some amazing stuff. When OpenAI released Astra this past September, University of California, Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg and his students saw demos that showcased its ability to render 3D images. They wondered if it could help with the simulations required to train different kinds of robots. These simulations need to be incredibly detailed and extremely accurate to ensure that sophisticated behavior—a humanoid that can dance or a robot hand that can grasp—will transfer faithfully to the real world.

One member of Goldberg’s lab gave Astra access to an Nvidia tool called Newton, showed it a video clip of a real robot in action, and asked if it could create a simulation of the scene.

“What blew us all away was that within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set—the position of the camera, the lighting, the background, all the materials,” Goldberg tells me.

Astra is also able to automate much of the drudgery involved with training a robot in simulation, Goldberg says, by running experiments and examining the results.

This is precisely what I found while training the virtual Microduck. Along with GPT-6 Sol, I used an agentic harness from Nous Research called Hermes and a Nvidia DGX Spark, a personal computer that contains a powerful AI chip.

I’ve previously written about using agents and coding models to configure, program, and debug physical robots. Normally, this kind of work requires significant expertise; modern coding models make it a cinch. But OpenAI’s newest model went far beyond just writing code.

It used a piece of Nvidia software called Isaac Sim to feed instructions to a model that controlled the virtual robot, watch videos of it in action to assess how well things were working, and suggest tweaks to its training regime.

This process allowed me to train the Microduck to walk around without toppling over. I initially tried getting GPT-6 Sol to teach the robot to moonwalk—I fed it a GIF of Michael Jackson sliding across the stage, which it tried to copy—but after hours of effort, it only resulted in a very jaunty backward jog. (The robots don’t have us totally beat quite yet.)

Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia who has collaborated with Goldberg, says the way AI can now control robots mirrors how software agents function. LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer.

This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others open sourced an agentic framework for robots called Aspire, which allows a robot to discover and use new skills. One example: GPT-6 Astra figured out how to use a pair of robot arms to solve a Rubik’s cube.

“It picks it up, tries to twist it, but has the wrong angle,” Fan says. “Then it reasons for a very, very long time, but it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time.”

At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), held in Austin, Texas, this week, Fan gave a keynote speech in which he talked about the incredible realization that AI models can automate a lot of the work needed to have a robot do sophisticated things. Fan showed off a demo in which Astra was put in control of a robot arm and told to paint a picture of the Golden Gate Bridge. Using some paint and brushes nearby, it duly completed the task.

Of course, getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult, requiring significant engineering expertise. The vision system on my robot duck does not work well enough to be deployed in a real product.

Still, the ease and speed of training robots with AI could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce, and Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown an interest in the approach.

Much like vibe coding a few years ago, we may well see breakthroughs in “vibe robotics” as hobbyists and engineers realize how easy it is to program and train robots. And, assuming I can perfect my robot helper, Leona may never have to go without treats again.
